articles.title: Open Visiting Policy and Delirium in Adult Patients in ICUs: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials.
articles.summary: To critically evaluate the comparative effects of open or flexible family presence policies vs. restricted or traditional family presence policies on the occurrence of delirium and other major outcomes among adult patients admitted to ICUs. We included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing open or flexible vs. restricted ICU visiting policies in adult patients. Thirteen RCTs comprising 3861 patients were included. Random-effects models showed that compared with restricted policies, open/flexible family presence reduced delirium occurrence (risk ratio [RR], 0.48; 95% CI, 0.29-0.81; low certainty) and IMV duration (mean difference [MD], -0.36 d; 95% CI, -0.46 to -0.26 d; low certainty). The intervention did not affect the ICU length of stay (MD, 4.21 d; 95% CI, -4.65 to 13.07 d; very low certainty), the rates of hospital-acquired infections (RR, 1.00; 95% CI, 0.81-1.23; low certainty), or ICU mortality (RR, 0.88; 95% CI, 0.72-1.08; very low certainty).

articles.title: Heterogeneity of Treatment Effect by Molecular Endotype in Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome: A Systematic Review.
articles.source: Annals of the American Thoracic Society
articles.summary: Eleven secondary analyses from ten RCTs (5,514 participants) were included. Despite numerous randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), few have identified effective therapies. One reason may be heterogeneity of treatment effect (HTE), in which distinct subgroups respond differently to the same intervention, potentially reflective of underlying biological endotypes. We conducted a systematic review to evaluate effect modification by molecular endotype across randomized ARDS trials and assess credibility of reported subgroup effects. In doing so, we aim to expose current knowledge gaps in how subgroups are defined and inform future clinical practice guideline recommendations.

articles.title: Isoflurane-Based Inhaled Sedation in Mechanically Ventilated Adults With Acute Hypoxemic Respiratory Failure: The SAVE-ICU Randomized Clinical Trial.
articles.summary: Adults (≥18 years) receiving sedation for less than 72 hours and receiving mechanical ventilation for AHRF from non-COVID respiratory failure (ratio of partial pressure of arterial oxygen [Pao2] to fraction of inspired oxygen [Fio2] <300 mm Hg) or COVID-19 were enrolled between September 2020 and March 2025 with follow-up through June 2025. Patients were randomized to an inhaled sedation strategy using isoflurane with intravenous adjuncts as clinically needed or to a usual intravenous sedation care strategy. Sedatives were titrated to achieve the desired target sedation score guided by clinical teams and continued until extubation or death. Of 786 patients randomized, 780 were included in the primary analysis (mean age, 61.1 years; 34.0% female; 73.7% non-COVID AHRF, mean Pao2:Fio2 ratio, 152.6 mm Hg); 385 in the inhaled sedation and 395 in the intravenous sedation groups. In the inhaled sedation group, 49.9% to 55.4% of patients received concomitant intravenous sedation on any day during the first 14 days after randomization.

pico.comparator: usual care intravenous sedation strategy in mechanically ventilated adults with AHRF. Pragmatic, effectiveness, open-lab
pico.outcomes: Primary outcome was all-cause hospital mortality. Secondary outcomes included ICU- and ventilator-free days at day 30; hospital-free days at day 60; use of refractory hypoxemia adjunctive therapies; delirium- and coma-free days at day 14; and quality-of-life and disability scores at 3 months.

In the inhaled sedation group, 49.9% to 55.4% of patients received concomitant intravenous sedation on any day during the first 14 days after randomization.

At hospital discharge, 161 of 379 patients (42.5%) in the inhaled sedation group had died, compared with 171 of 390 patients (43.8%) in the intravenous sedation group (risk ratio, 0.98 [95% CI, 0.84 to 1.14]; P = .85).

The inhaled sedation group received more adjunctive therapies for hypoxemia (239 [63.9%] vs 214 [55.0%]; between-group difference, 8.89% [95% CI, 1.95% to 15.83%]) and had fewer delirium- and coma-free days (between-group difference, -0.95 [95% CI, -1.69 to -0.22]).

Check randomization, concealment, blinding, missing data, and whether analysis was intention-to-treat.
